one_liner: Header-only counter-based CPU/GPU RNG family (Philox, Threefry, ARS); only AES-NI variants clearly beat std::mt19937_64.
what_it_does: Random123 is a header-only family of counter-based pseudorandom generators (Threefry, Philox, ARS/AESNI) that compute result = rng(counter, key) as a stateless keyed bijection instead of advancing mutable internal state like std::mt19937_64. The C/C++ APIs return a fixed-size array (r123arrayNxW) from an explicit counter and key rather than exposing an operator()-based engine; the bundled r123::Engine<CBRNG> template adapts any generator to the C++11 UniformRandomNumberEngine interface so it can back <random> distributions. CUDA, OpenCL, and Metal kernel code ship alongside the C/C++ headers for GPU use.
how_it_is_fast: Because each call is a pure function of (counter, key) with no state to read-modify-write, the generators vectorize and parallelize trivially and avoid the roughly 2.5KB of per-thread state std::mt19937 needs. ARS and AESNI reuse the hardware AES-NI round function directly, so on supporting CPUs ARS-7 needs only about 1.1 cycles/byte (ARS-5 about 0.7). Threefry (ARX rounds derived from the Skein/Threefish hash) and Philox (Feistel network plus one wide integer multiply per round) get most of their speed from a handful of cheap integer ops per output word rather than a large state-shuffle step.
when_to_use: Monte Carlo / stochastic simulation workloads needing millions of independent, reproducible streams addressed by (counter,key) instead of stored per-thread generator state
CUDA/OpenCL/Metal GPU kernels or heavily multithreaded CPU code, where per-thread state size and synchronization matter more than single-core throughput
x86 CPUs with AES-NI, where ARS-7/ARS-5 give a real ~1.8x-2.9x throughput win over std::mt19937_64 (11.1-17.8 GB/s vs 6.1 GB/s)
Checkpoint/restart or exact cross-run/cross-platform reproducibility, since output depends only on (counter,key), not call history
when_not_to_use: CPU-only code without AES-NI and no tolerance for a marginal win: the portable Threefry-4x64-20 is only about 1.05x std::mt19937_64 (6.4 vs 6.1 GB/s), and several Philox variants are slower than mt19937_64 on CPU
Code needing a true drop-in std::mt19937/std::mt19937_64 replacement without writing adapter code; the native call shape rng(counter,key) differs from a stateful engine's operator()
Cryptography or security-sensitive randomness: the README explicitly states these CBRNGs, despite being built from cipher-like primitives, are not suitable for crypto
Projects wanting active upstream support: last commit on main was 2022-01-17, and open issues (NVCC optimization flags, RISC-V/LoongArch/HIP ports) have sat unanswered since 2022-2023

integration.dependencies: none for the core library; GNU Scientific Library only if using the optional gsl_cbrng/gsl_microrng adapters or the ut_gsl test
integration.min_toolchain: a reasonable C99 (C API) or C++98 compiler per tests/README; C++11 needed for the SeedSeq-based seed() overloads in r123::Engine; AES-NI-capable CPU plus compiler intrinsics needed for the ARS/AESNI speedups
integration.platforms: x86 (AES-NI required for ARS/AESNI's advantage; a 64-bit-producing-128-bit multiply is needed for the Nx64 Philox variants); also ships CUDA, OpenCL, and Metal kernel code; ARM/RISC-V/LoongArch/HIP support is requested in open issues but not confirmed working
integration.thread_safety: not documented as an explicit guarantee; the core CBRNG functors are stateless pure functions of (counter,key), so concurrent calls with distinct counters are safe by construction, but the stateful r123::Engine<> wrapper's thread safety is not documented
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — explain: the native CBRNG call rng(counter,key) is not drop-in for std::mt19937_64; the bundled r123::Engine<CBRNG> template wraps any generator to satisfy the C++11 UniformRandomNumberEngine interface so it can back <random> distributions, but the application must still pick and construct the generator explicitly.

gotchas: Engine<CBRNG>'s copy constructor calls fix_invariant() to recompute a cached output block when a sentinel (v.back()!=0) is set — an internal correctness detail worth knowing before subclassing or serializing it
AESNI/ARS key_type is opaque and must be built from a separate ukey_type via key construction, unlike Threefry/Philox keys which can be used directly
Philox's Nx64 forms only compile/run on hardware and compilers that support 64-bit multiplication producing a 128-bit result; Nx32 forms are the portable fallback
README notes Random123 has been reported to use 16 bytes of static memory per CUDA thread, unintentionally, with no workaround given
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Random123 (ARS-7) over PCG/xoshiro/biski64/AESRand when the workload specifically needs stateless, independently-addressable (counter,key) streams for parallel/GPU Monte Carlo or exact reproducibility across runs; for plain single-threaded CPU throughput with a conventional stateful RNG API, PCG-cpp, wjakob/pcg32, xoshiro_cpp, or biski64 all show larger and more portable speedups over std::mt19937(_64) without requiring AES-NI hardware.
verified_claims_summary: In the peer-reviewed SC11 paper's Table 2 (confirmed directly from the PDF), on a 3.07GHz quad-core Xeon X5667 (Westmere) with gcc 4.5.3 and no stated optimization flags, std::mt19937_64 (the C++0x/libstdc++ engine) ran at 6.1 GB/s; the AES-NI-accelerated ARS-7 reached 11.1 GB/s (~1.8x) and ARS-5 reached 17.8 GB/s (~2.9x), while the portable, no-special-hardware Threefry-4x64-20 reached 6.4 GB/s, only a marginal ~1.05x.
status_note: Abandoned: the last commit on main was 2022-01-17 (the repo's 2024-02-15 pushed_at is only a push/metadata timestamp, not a new commit) and several issues opened in 2022-2023 (NVCC optimization flags, new-architecture ports) remain unaddressed; still BSD-3-Clause licensed and header-only, so it is trivial to vendor and freeze regardless of upstream activity.
